blocks.content: Whether a server remembers anything about a client between one request and the next is one of the most consequential decisions in system design, because it determines whether that server can be freely duplicated, replaced, and load balanced across, or whether every request from a given client has to keep finding its way back to one specific machine. That single property, stateless or stateful, shapes almost everything else about how a service can be scaled and operated.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285852452-383056150.png
blocks.alt: A stateless service keeps nothing important in its own memory, so a load balancer can send any request to any instance, with a shared external store holding whatever state actually exists

blocks.content: 1. What Stateless Means

A stateless service treats every incoming request as complete and self-contained, needing nothing remembered from any previous request to handle it correctly. Whatever context is required, who the user is, what they were doing, gets included in the request itself or fetched fresh from an external store, rather than being kept in the memory of whichever server happens to be handling it.

This does not mean the system as a whole has no data or memory, only that this particular service does not hold it locally. A stateless web server can absolutely be backed by a database full of persistent data, the statelessness refers specifically to the server process itself, not to the system it is part of.

A simple test that cuts through most confusion here is imagining a request being handled by a completely different, freshly started instance with no history at all. If it would still work correctly, the handler is genuinely stateless. If it depends on something only the original instance happens to know, it is not, no matter how the code is organized.

This is also why stateless services are sometimes described as disposable or cattle rather than pets, a slightly blunt but genuinely useful way of remembering that no individual instance is precious or irreplaceable, since none of them are holding anything the system cannot immediately get from somewhere else.
2. What Stateful Means

A stateful service keeps something important in its own memory or on its own local disk between requests, information that only exists on that specific instance and would be lost, or at least unavailable elsewhere, if that instance disappeared. A database holding its actual data on local disk is stateful. A server keeping an in-progress user session in memory between requests is stateful, even if that seems like a small, temporary thing to hold onto.

The defining test is simple: if this specific instance were destroyed right now, would something be lost or unreachable that a different, freshly started instance could not immediately provide instead. A stateful service answers yes to that question; a stateless one answers no.

It is worth separating stateful from merely slow to restart. A service that takes time to warm up a local cache after starting is not necessarily stateful in the sense this topic cares about, as long as nothing is permanently lost, only temporarily slower, when that warm-up has to happen again on a fresh instance.

This test also explains why a cache, even though it typically holds data that can be rebuilt from a database if lost, still counts as stateful in the practical sense that matters for scaling: losing it does not lose the data permanently, but it does lose something, performance, that the rest of the system was depending on it to provide.
3. Why Statelessness Enables Horizontal Scaling

This distinction is really the deeper mechanism behind why horizontal scaling, covered in the vertical versus horizontal scaling topic, works so cleanly for some services and requires real engineering effort for others. A stateless service can be scaled out by simply running more identical copies behind a load balancer, since any instance can correctly handle any request, with nothing instance-specific to worry about losing or misrouting.

A stateful service resists this. Adding a second instance does not automatically double its capacity the way it does for a stateless service, because the two instances do not automatically share whatever state each is holding, and requests that depend on a specific piece of state have to somehow find their way back to whichever instance actually has it.

This is not a minor implementation detail, it is frequently the single decision that determines whether a scaling problem is solved by an afternoon of adding instances or by weeks of re-architecting how a service handles the state it currently keeps to itself.
3.1 Statelessness Is A Property Of A Layer, Not A Whole System
blocks.text: 3.1 Statelessness Is A Property Of A Layer, Not A Whole System

blocks.content: It helps to think of a real system as a stack of layers, some stateless and some stateful, rather than asking whether the whole system is one or the other. The application tier handling incoming requests is very often made stateless deliberately, while the cache and database layers underneath it remain fully stateful, holding the actual data the stateless tier reads and writes on every request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396523087-39375405.png
blocks.alt: A stateless application tier commonly sits on top of stateful cache and database layers that actually hold the data

blocks.content: This layered view is what makes the earlier claim make sense that statelessness does not mean a system has no memory at all. It means the specific layer in question, usually the one that needs to scale out the most aggressively, has pushed its memory down into a layer built specifically to hold it well.
3.2 The Deployment Benefit People Underrate

Beyond raw scaling, statelessness has a second, quieter benefit that shows up constantly in day-to-day operations: deployments and instance replacement become trivial. A stateless instance can simply be terminated and replaced with a fresh one at any moment, since it was never holding anything that only existed there.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285857302-676595117.png
blocks.alt: A stateless instance can be killed and replaced freely during a deployment; a stateful one first needs its state drained or migrated somewhere safe

blocks.content: This is what makes rolling deployments, where old instances are replaced with new ones a few at a time with zero downtime, straightforward for a stateless tier and genuinely difficult for a stateful one, which needs an explicit plan for what happens to whatever state a terminated instance was holding.

This same property is what makes an entirely different instance type, like a spot or preemptible cloud instance that can be reclaimed by the provider with little notice, a genuinely safe cost-saving option for a stateless tier, while using the same cheap, interruptible instance type for a stateful workload would be reckless.
4. Where Does The State Go

Making a service stateless does not make the state it depended on disappear, it just moves that state somewhere external and shared: a database, a distributed cache, or a dedicated session store that every instance can reach equally, rather than the memory of any one particular server.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285859234-977621517.png
blocks.alt: A stateless instance reads whatever state it needs from a shared external store at the start of a request and writes any changes back at the end, rather than holding it locally between requests

blocks.content: This is the actual mechanical trick behind statelessness: the application code is written as if it remembers nothing, and every piece of context it needs gets fetched from, and written back to, a shared store that every instance can reach identically. The instance itself becomes disposable; the state becomes the external store problem to keep available and fast.

Which external store is right depends entirely on the shape of the state being moved. Something that needs to survive forever and be queried in complex ways belongs in a database. Something that is disposable, rebuildable, and needed mostly for speed belongs in a cache. Treating every kind of externalized state as interchangeable is itself a common mistake worth avoiding.
4.1 Reacting To A Traffic Spike
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285861153-192240524.png
blocks.alt: A stateless tier can absorb a traffic spike by simply adding instances; a stateful one has to solve where the new instance state comes from first

blocks.content: This difference is exactly why autoscaling, covered in the vertical versus horizontal scaling topic, is such a natural fit for stateless tiers and such an awkward fit for stateful ones. Adding a stateless instance in response to a spike works immediately, with the new instance reaching the same shared external store as every other instance. Adding a stateful instance, like a new database replica or cache node, means that instance starts with nothing and needs a real process to catch up before it is genuinely useful.

This is also why capacity planning conversations for a stateless tier tend to be simpler and more mechanical, mostly a question of how many identical instances to run, while capacity planning for a stateful layer, like a database or cache cluster, has to account for data distribution, replication, and rebalancing on top of raw instance count.
5. Session Affinity As A Workaround
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285863017-211519359.png
blocks.alt: If session state lives only in one instance memory, a request that lands on a different instance simply cannot find it

blocks.content: Before, or instead of, externalizing state properly, a common shortcut is session affinity, also called sticky sessions: the load balancer is configured to always route a given client back to the same specific instance, so that instance in-memory state keeps working correctly for that client. This is the same mechanism covered for WebSocket connections in the long polling versus WebSockets topic, applied here to ordinary HTTP session state instead of an open connection.

Sticky sessions solve the immediate problem cheaply, with no architecture change needed, but they reintroduce exactly the fragility statelessness was meant to remove: if that one specific instance goes down, every client pinned to it loses their session state entirely, and the load balancer now has an uneven, harder-to-reason-about routing job instead of being able to send any request anywhere.

Sticky sessions also complicate load balancing itself, since the load balancer can no longer freely send traffic to whichever instance currently has the most spare capacity. An instance that happens to be pinned to an unusually large number of active sessions ends up overloaded while others sit comparatively idle, a problem a purely stateless design never has to think about at all.

Sticky sessions are still a reasonable, deliberate choice in one specific situation: a genuine migration step on the way toward full statelessness, buying time to externalize state properly without blocking a horizontal scaling effort that needs to start now. Treating it as a permanent destination rather than a temporary bridge is where it becomes an anti-pattern.
6. Idempotency And Statelessness

A closely related but distinct property is idempotency: whether making the same request multiple times produces the same result as making it once. A stateless service can still be non-idempotent, for example a stateless payment endpoint that charges a card every time it is called, regardless of whether it remembers anything between calls.

The two properties matter together in practice because retries are common in distributed systems, a client timing out and trying again, a load balancer retrying a failed request against a different instance, and a stateless, idempotent endpoint handles that retry safely and correctly, while a stateless but non-idempotent one can cause real damage, like a duplicate charge, even though statelessness itself was never the problem.

It is worth stating the relationship precisely rather than treating the two as synonyms: statelessness is about what a service remembers, idempotency is about what happens when the same operation is repeated. A service can be either, both, or neither, and a design review should check for each one separately rather than assuming one implies the other.
6.1 A Concrete Idempotency Pattern

The standard way to make an otherwise unsafe endpoint like a payment charge safe to retry is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key for the logical operation once, sends it with every attempt including retries, and the server checks whether that key has already been processed before doing the work again.

blocks.title: This still needs a stateful lookup somewhere
blocks.content: Notice the handler itself remains stateless, holding nothing in its own memory, but it depends on a shared, persistent record of which idempotency keys have already been processed. The statelessness of the handler and the need for a durable, shared record of prior attempts are not in conflict, they are exactly the pattern this whole topic describes.

The idempotency key itself has to come from somewhere sensible too. A client generating a fresh key on every retry defeats the entire purpose, so the key is normally generated once per logical operation, before the first attempt, and reused unchanged across every retry of that same attempt.
7. The Cost Of Externalizing State

Moving state out of local memory into a shared external store is not free. What used to be a fast, in-process memory read becomes a network call to a database or cache, adding real latency to a request that previously paid none. This trade is almost always worth it for the scaling and reliability gained, but it is a genuine cost, not a free architectural upgrade.

A JSON web token is a clever way of avoiding some of that cost for authentication specifically: rather than looking up a server-side session on every request, the client carries a signed token containing its own claims, and the server only has to verify the signature, no external lookup needed at all. This pushes the state onto the client itself, which works well for authentication claims but is not a general substitute for externalizing every kind of session state, since a token cannot hold data that needs to be revoked instantly or that is too large or sensitive to hand to the client.
7.1 Tokens Trade Away Instant Revocation

The signed-token approach to authentication has a real limitation worth naming alongside its benefits: because the server never looks anything up to validate the token, there is no natural place to instantly revoke one. A stolen or compromised token remains valid until it expires, no matter what the server learns in the meantime, unless extra infrastructure is added specifically to track revoked tokens.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285865130-931600560.png
blocks.alt: A server-side session can be deleted to revoke access instantly; a signed token remains valid until it naturally expires unless a separate revocation list is maintained

blocks.title: The usual compromise
blocks.content: Many systems keep token lifetimes short, minutes rather than days, and pair them with a separate refresh mechanism, accepting a small window of continued validity after a compromise in exchange for avoiding a server-side lookup on every single request.

Some systems split the difference by keeping tokens mostly self-contained but checking a small, fast-to-query revocation list on top, accepting one lightweight lookup in exchange for the ability to revoke access immediately when it genuinely matters, such as a user changing their password after a suspected compromise.
8. Stateful Services That Are Hard To Avoid
blocks.text: 8. Stateful Services That Are Hard To Avoid

blocks.content: Not everything can be made stateless, and pretending otherwise leads to bad designs. A database has to be stateful somewhere, since its entire purpose is durably holding data, and that data has to physically live on some disk, on some machine, even if it is replicated for safety. An in-memory cache is stateful by definition, its entire value comes from holding hot data in memory rather than fetching it fresh every time.

A WebSocket connection, covered in depth elsewhere, is inherently stateful too: the open socket itself only exists on whichever server accepted it. The realistic goal in most systems is not eliminating statefulness everywhere, it is being deliberate about which components are stateful, keeping that set as small as possible, and making the rest, usually the bulk of the application tier, cleanly stateless.

Recognizing which components fall into this unavoidably stateful category early, during initial design rather than after a scaling problem forces the question, changes how much operational investment gets planned for them from the start: replication, backup, and failover strategy for a database, cluster topology for a cache, connection distribution for long-lived sockets, all decided deliberately rather than retrofitted under pressure.
9. A Worked Example

Consider a shopping cart. An early, simple implementation might keep the cart contents in the memory of whichever server the user session started on, which works fine with one server and breaks the moment a second server is added, since a request landing on the other instance sees an empty cart.

The fix is moving the cart into a shared store, a database row or a cache entry keyed by user id, that any instance can read and write. The application server handling the request becomes fully interchangeable, any instance can serve any user request, while the actual cart data lives in the one place designed to hold it reliably and share it across every instance equally.
9.1 What Changes Operationally

Before externalizing the cart, losing an application instance meant every user whose session happened to be pinned to it lost their cart contents entirely, a real, visible failure from the user perspective. After externalizing it, losing an instance loses nothing, since the cart never lived there in the first place, only a brief interruption while the load balancer routes around the lost instance.

This is the concrete, felt difference between the two designs during an actual incident, not just an abstract architectural preference. It is also a good illustration of why this decision matters more the larger and more failure-prone the fleet of instances becomes, since a small, stable single-server setup rarely experiences this failure mode often enough to notice.

The same argument extends naturally to how the shared cart store itself gets scaled, which is really the read replicas and connection pooling material covered elsewhere in this section applied to a concrete, relatable feature rather than an abstract database example.
10. Common Anti-Patterns

["Keeping session or request-specific state in application server memory and then trying to scale horizontally without addressing it.","Reaching for sticky sessions as a permanent fix rather than a stopgap on the way to properly externalized state.","Assuming a stateless service can be treated as fully disposable and idempotent without checking whether it actually is idempotent.","Externalizing state to a single database with no thought given to that database becoming the new bottleneck or single point of failure."]
items: Keeping session or request-specific state in application server memory and then trying to scale horizontally without addressing it.
Reaching for sticky sessions as a permanent fix rather than a stopgap on the way to properly externalized state.
Assuming a stateless service can be treated as fully disposable and idempotent without checking whether it actually is idempotent.
Externalizing state to a single database with no thought given to that database becoming the new bottleneck or single point of failure.

blocks.content: 10.1 A Practical Checklist

["List everything a request handler currently keeps in memory or on local disk between requests.","For each item, decide whether it truly needs to survive an instance restart or being load balanced to a different machine.","Move anything that does into a shared external store reachable by every instance equally.","Confirm the resulting stateless endpoints are also idempotent wherever retries are possible."]
items: List everything a request handler currently keeps in memory or on local disk between requests.
For each item, decide whether it truly needs to survive an instance restart or being load balanced to a different machine.
Move anything that does into a shared external store reachable by every instance equally.
Confirm the resulting stateless endpoints are also idempotent wherever retries are possible.

blocks.content: Running this checklist during a design review, before code is written rather than after a scaling incident forces the conversation, is a cheap habit that catches most of the anti-patterns listed above well before they become a production problem.
11. Real-World Examples

{"headers":["System","Statefulness"],"rows":[["Stateless REST API tier","Session and user data live in a database or cache; any instance can handle any request"],["Token-based authentication","Client carries a signed token, avoiding a server-side session lookup entirely"],["Primary relational database","Inherently stateful; its entire purpose is durably holding data on disk"],["WebSocket or long-polling server","Stateful for the lifetime of each open connection, requiring sticky routing or a backplane"]]}

Notice that the table lists two rows that look similar at a glance, a stateless API tier and token-based authentication, but they are really the same underlying idea applied at two different points in the stack: one keeps the request handler itself free of memory, the other keeps the authentication step specifically free of a server-side lookup.

A useful pattern across almost every row in this table is that the stateful component is also the one that gets the most deliberate operational attention, replication, monitoring, careful capacity planning, while the stateless layer around it is comparatively easy to operate precisely because it was designed to be interchangeable from the start.
12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: This distinction comes up in nearly every system design interview because it directly determines how a component can be scaled, and a strong answer explicitly identifies which pieces of a proposed system are stateless and which are unavoidably stateful, rather than treating the whole system as one uniform blob. Naming where session or request state actually lives, and how any instance can reach it, shows the same architectural clarity rewarded throughout system design interviews generally.

It is also worth being ready to discuss the trade-off directly: externalizing state adds a network hop and a dependency on the external store being available and fast, and a thoughtful answer weighs that cost against the scaling flexibility gained rather than presenting statelessness as an unconditional good with no downside at all.
A stateless service has not eliminated state. It has simply refused to be the one holding it.

Bringing the deployment and traffic-spike angles covered earlier into an interview answer, not just the scaling angle, is a reliable way to show this topic has been thought through operationally rather than only architecturally.
12.1 A Common Follow-Up Question

A frequent follow-up asks how you would migrate an existing stateful service, one holding session data in memory, to a stateless design without downtime. A grounded answer introduces the external store first, writes to both the local memory and the external store during a transition period, switches reads over to the external store once confidence is high, and only then removes the local in-memory state entirely, verifying at each step rather than cutting over all at once.

blocks.title: Why the interviewer asks this
blocks.content: Almost no real system gets to design statelessness in from a blank slate. Describing a safe migration path shows the same practical judgment valued throughout this section, rather than only being able to describe the ideal end state.

A second common follow-up asks whether a stateless design is ever the wrong choice. It is, whenever the network cost of reaching an external store on every single request outweighs the benefit, for an extremely latency-sensitive, low-throughput internal tool a simple stateful design with no scaling ambitions at all can genuinely be the more sensible engineering choice.

Keep the single restart test from earlier close at hand when reviewing a design: if killing any one instance right now would lose or strand something important, that component is stateful, and the question worth asking next is whether it needs to be, or whether that state can be pushed somewhere built to hold it properly.
Key Takeaways

["A stateless service needs nothing remembered from previous requests; a stateful one keeps something important locally between requests.","Statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling simple, since any instance can handle any request with nothing instance-specific at risk.","Externalizing state moves it to a shared store like a database or cache, trading a small latency cost for scaling and reliability.","Sticky sessions are a common workaround but reintroduce the fragility statelessness was meant to avoid.","Some components, like databases, caches, and long-lived connections, are inherently stateful, and the goal is minimizing and isolating that set rather than eliminating it entirely."]
items: A stateless service needs nothing remembered from previous requests; a stateful one keeps something important locally between requests.
Statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling simple, since any instance can handle any request with nothing instance-specific at risk.
Externalizing state moves it to a shared store like a database or cache, trading a small latency cost for scaling and reliability.
Sticky sessions are a common workaround but reintroduce the fragility statelessness was meant to avoid.
Some components, like databases, caches, and long-lived connections, are inherently stateful, and the goal is minimizing and isolating that set rather than eliminating it entirely.
